newsitem.title: INDIA: India's RBI injects liquidity into banking system.
newsitem.headline: India's RBI injects liquidity into banking system.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Saturday signalled a cut in interest rates by announcing reduced banks' cash reserve ratios and deposit interest rates.
The RBI, unveiling its second half 1996/97 monetary policy, said it was cutting the cash reserve ratio (CRR) on banks to 10 percent from 12 percent to be implemented in four stages.
Simultaneously, it cut the interest cap on term deposits of 30 days to one year maturity to 10 percent from 11 percent.

Each percentage point cut in CRR would augment banks' lendable resources by 42.75 billion rupees, RBI said. The cut in term deposit rates would help banks to maintain their spreads despite a cut in lending rates.

In recent statements, the RBI has emphasised the need to cut lending rates to reverse a declining trend in banks' credit to industry. Prime lending rates now range from 15.5 to 19.0 percent per annum.

The RBI also set an interest rate cap of 15 percent per annum on export credit. Earlier, banks were free to fix interest rate on export credit beyond 90 days, and many banks were charging rates as high as 19 percent, exporters had said.
"The decline in non-food credit during 1996/97 (April-March) so far needs to be corrected," the RBI said.

"Besides exports, banks need to pay particular attention to agriculture and small-scale industries," it said. It said banks have already been advised to increase disbursements for agriculture by 25 percent during the current financial year.
For the first time, the RBI is also allowing banks to buy shares from the secondary market within limits. Banks are now allowed to buy only from the primary market.
Analysts said this step would release about 30 billion rupees for bank purchases in primary/secondary market.
The RBI also allowed banks to lend to Indian firms out of expatriate Indians' foreign exchange deposits, further boosting liquidity in the inter-bank forex market.
This is expected to encourage banks to attract more expatriate dollar deposits, analysts said.
The RBI said it was also exempting oilseeds, oils, sugar and cotton from selective credit controls following an improved supply of these commodities.

"In the context of the favourable supply situation, all the above mentioned commodities, except buffer stock and the unreleased stocks of sugar to sugar mills, are exempted from all stipulations of selective credit controls effective October 21," it said.
Presently bank advances against pulses, coarse foodgrains, oilseeds and oils, sugar and cotton are subject to selective credit controls.
Traders have been complaining of low trading volumes in commodities because of the credit sqeeze.
